sources.text:
Trump administration pauses border wall construction in Big Bend National Park amid criticism
The project has drawn opposition from both Democrats and Republicans over its potential environmental, cultural, and economic impact
One of the most controversial projects in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has been temporarily put on hold after bulldozers and other heavy machinery began altering the landscape of Big Bend National Park in Texas. The decision to halt the work comes after weeks of criticism, protests, and lawsuits over plans to expand border infrastructure in one of the most remote areas along the U.S.-Mexico border.
Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Commissioner Rodney Scott announced Monday that all construction activities inside the park would be suspended while he travels to the area to conduct a personal evaluation and meet with local authorities, residents, and other affected stakeholders.
“CBP is pausing all construction activity in Big Bend National Park while I visit and conduct a personal, on-the-ground evaluation,” Scott said in a post on X. The official said the agency is committed to national security but also to protecting places such as Big Bend.
The pause came after images of bulldozers working inside the park triggered a new wave of questions about the project. The machinery began clearing land for work that includes patrol roads and barriers designed to prevent vehicles from crossing, although the administration had previously ruled out building the 30-foot steel bollard wall that is planned for other parts of the region inside the park.
The work is part of a much broader expansion of border infrastructure under Trump. Congress allocated about $46.5 billion for construction and expansion of the border wall in legislation the president signed in July 2025.
In the so-called Big Bend sector, the plans include a 9.1-meter (30-foot) steel bollard barrier in areas west of the national park, along with roughly 322 kilometers (200 miles) of patrol roads and 27 kilometers (17 miles) of vehicle barriers at specific locations. Another 266 kilometers (165 miles) of vehicle barriers are planned east of the park. The total cost of the project in the region could exceed $7 billion.
Although CBP decided not to build the traditional wall inside the national park and nearby Big Bend Ranch State Park, the work that has begun has generated much of the controversy. Critics have particularly questioned the need to open new roads in an area where rugged terrain already makes border crossings difficult.
The Big Bend sector covers roughly one-quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border but accounts for around only 1% of migrant apprehensions, partly because of its mountains, canyons, and vast desert areas.
Opposition that crosses party lines
Opposition to the project has become one of the few areas of Trump’s border agenda where Republicans and Democrats have found common ground.
Republican Texas Sen. John Cornyn called on Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to halt the work, arguing that Big Bend’s terrain already represents a significant natural obstacle for people attempting to cross the border.
Several Republican sheriffs in the region have also spoken out against the project. Thaddeus Cleveland, sheriff of Terrell County and a former Border Patrol agent, believes the strategy should be adapted to the particular conditions of each sector and has advocated for greater use of technology instead of physical barriers.
Opposition also includes Democratic lawmakers, residents, business owners, former National Park Service officials and environmental organizations.
For critics, the problem goes far beyond the project’s visual impact. Construction could affect archaeological areas, sacred Indigenous sites, wildlife migration routes and the landscape on which much of the region’s tourism industry depends.
Business owners who organize river trips and other activities inside the park fear that construction could alter precisely the remote, natural character that attracts visitors.
Indigenous groups have also warned of potential damage to places used for religious purposes. One of the lawsuits filed against the project argues that construction could make it more difficult to access traditional sites used by the Lipan Apache Tribe.
The administration has accelerated the work after waiving or setting aside several regulations designed to protect environmental, historical, and cultural resources. At least four lawsuits have sought to halt different parts of the project in the Big Bend region.
For now, it remains unclear how long the suspension will last or whether it will substantially alter the Trump administration’s plans. Scott has said he expects the first layer of the border wall to be built by the end of next year.

CBP pauses bulldozers in Big Bend National Park
There will be a “pause on all activity in that park,” CBP officials said
What happened
The Trump administration on Monday said it was temporarily halting construction on a contentious border project in Texas’ Big Bend National Park. In a video on social media, Customs and Border Protection chief Rodney Scott said he had “put a pause on all activity in that park, as far as construction goes, until I can get down there” to West Texas to “do a personal evaluation” and “talk to some stakeholders.”
Who said what
Scott’s announcement “comes amid massive outcry from local residents, businesses and law enforcement officials,” The Texas Tribune said, and “bipartisan frustration” over CBP’s shifting accounts of its plans for the treasured national park. CBP earlier this year “backed off plans to build a 30-foot-tall bollard wall” through Big Bend, The Associated Press said. But it is “still moving forward with other border protection measures such as a new road, lights” and vehicle barriers.
The deployment of bulldozers last week drew “national attention and bipartisan criticism” from across Texas over the project’s “speed” and “seeming disregard for a prized piece of untrammeled wilderness,” The New York Times said. Local sheriffs argue the project is “costly and unnecessary in a desolate and undeveloped area where few migrants have ever crossed.” The CBP’s Big Bend Sector “covers a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border,” CNN said, but “sees only about 1% of border apprehensions.”

sources.news_title: Trump Admin Caves On 'Insane' Bulldozing Of Big Bend National Park
sources.text:
The Trump administration has halted bulldozing inside Big Bend National Park after a wave of bipartisan opposition over construction in one of Texas's most celebrated wilderness areas.
CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott announced the pause Monday, saying he had flown to Texas to conduct a personal evaluation of the terrain. The official said he would meet with local stakeholders and law enforcement before any further work proceeds.
The agency has budgeted $1.72 billion for the project, according to CNN.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection says the work includes one new road, upgraded existing roads, detection technology, and vehicle barriers.
"I just landed in Texas headed to Big Bend National Park," Scott said in a video posted Monday.
"Last night, I put a pause on all activity in that park as far as construction goes until I can get down there and do a personal evaluation, talk to some stakeholders, talk to local law enforcement in that area, and more to follow this week," he said.
Bulldozers entered the park on Aug. 6, CNN reported, clearing brush and uprooting trees near Santa Elena Canyon before Scott's announcement.
Scott had described the agency's activity to CNN as "survey and design work."
On X, Scott wrote that the project would involve "one new access road, improving existing roads, installing detection technology, and placing vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations."
Bob Krumenaker, who spent five years as Big Bend's superintendent and now chairs the Keep Big Bend Wild advocacy group, told CNN the entire plan is nothing short of "insane."
"If they continue with this and build most of the things they have talked about, or even a good fraction of those, this will be the biggest desecration of the national park system — not just Big Bend National Park — since they built a dam in a pristine valley in Yosemite National Park more than 100 years ago," Krumenaker said.
"This is a story that our children and grandchildren will be telling," he added. "It's just a tremendous erosion, if not violation, of the agreement that Texans and the American people made when they established that national park."
"This is purely political, and it will, it risks destroying one of the nation's greatest places."
The park accounts for only about 1% of apprehensions of unauthorized border crossers along the southern border, CNN noted.
Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin last week urging him to meet with local stakeholders before any further construction proceeds, the Texas Tribune reported.
Texas Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham (R-TX) sent a cease-and-desist letter in July to U.S. Customs and Border Protection after she said a federal contractor worked in Big Bend Ranch State Park without permission, according to CNN.

"CBP is pausing all construction activity in Big Bend National Park while I visit and conduct a personal, on-the-ground evaluation."
"CBP is firmly committed to protecting America," Scott continued, "and that includes our national treasures like Big Bend National Park (BBNP). We know the current and predictable national security threats and they are real. Now over the next couple of days, I will join a small team to evaluate the terrain and listen to local leadership, community members and stakeholders to ensure that we secure our borders while simultaneously protecting BBNP for generations to come."
Texas Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham sent a cease and desist letter to US Customs and Border Protection last month, saying that the administration was clearing ranch land without the General Land Office's say-so. Buckingham has spoken out against "a physical barrier in the Big Bend region," the Houston Chronicle reports, and is an advocate for Trump. She is currently up for reelection.
A bipartisan letter was also sent to Texas Governor Greg Abbott to encourage Trump to stop the construction project. Local elected leaders signed onto the letter and Texas GOP Senator John Cornyn sent his own letter weighing in, urging the construction to stop.
This comes as the Trump administration has not given up the fight to put a strong, physical barrier along the length of the US-Mexico border, which spans from Texas across New Mexico, Arizona and into California. At issue for Buckingham are the ranches in the area, which could be cut off from the river should the project go forward to completion. Other critics cite environmental concerns.
Locals have applauded efforts to block the project and to retain river access for affected ranches. Buckingham also told the Montana firm that's in the process of clearing and building to restore the land to its state before the work began.
Officials in the Big Bend area have said that they do not believe a border wall is necessary for the 118-mile stretch of land that borders the Mexican states of Coahuila and Chihuahua. The area, they say, is desolate and undeveloped and has not historically seen many illegal border crossers crossing into the US.
The Trump administration had been planning a 30-foot wall but is now instead building "a new access road along the border, installing detection technology and erecting vehicle barriers," The New York Times reports. Critics of even these border protection plans, such as the Center for Biological Diversity's Laiken Jordahl, say the damage already done is "irreversible." His group has brought a lawsuit to stop the border work.
The 4 years of the Biden administration saw a drastic increase in both legal and illegal crossings, with estimates saying that between 10 and 20 million people crossed into the US both illegally and under a variety of semi-legal programs put in place by the Biden administration to do just that. Illegal border crossings have fallen to near zero under Trump, who ran on a platform of halting illegal migration.

sources.news_title: Border construction paused at Big Bend National Park after public outcry
sources.text:
Border construction paused at Big Bend National Park after public outcry
U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott says he is "pausing all construction activity" on border infrastructure in Big Bend National Park, ahead of a visit to the area this week.
SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:
In west Texas, the Trump administration is temporarily stopping construction on a border infrastructure project in Big Bend National Park. The head of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Rodney Scott, said Monday he was pausing all construction activity in the park. He will be traveling to the region for a, quote, "personal evaluation." Travis Bubenik with Marfa Public Radio has been following this story all year and joins us this morning. Hi, Travis.
TRAVIS BUBENIK, BYLINE: Morning.
PFEIFFER: Some of our listeners may have seen the images of bulldozers clearing land and vegetation in the park earlier this month. What can you tell us about why this work is being stopped now?
BUBENIK: It's really just the result of a bipartisan pushback to this plan here in west Texas and across the state that's been bubbling up to the surface for, really, months now. People out here from local residents to leaders, to Republican and Democratic sheriffs across the region are just angry about these plans for new barriers and roads in this national park. I mean, almost the second the bulldozers showed up, there was just a lot of outrage about this across the state and the country. Just a few days ago, the CBP commissioner, Rodney Scott, initially defended the work, calling it survey and design work. But there's just been continued shock and anger at these images of, you know, heavy machinery cutting through the pristine desert out here in west Texas. And, again, there's a chorus of people in the region across political aisles that say the barriers are just not needed out here.
PFEIFFER: Travis, I understand that yesterday you took a flight over Big Bend. Tell us what you saw.
BUBENIK: We did, yeah. We got up in a little plane with a local pilot, hovered over these mountains for a while and tried to get eyes on what was going on in the park. And we did see a couple of construction sites where you could clearly see the crews had started cutting new paths into this untouched, rocky desert. But we also did see the heavy machinery idled, the work stopped. In fact, you know, seeing this region from the sky gives you a good sense of just how extremely remote and rugged it is. There are massive mountains that line either side of the Rio Grande, hardly any roads leading to the southern border from the Mexican side.
The landscape out here is simply too extreme for huge numbers of people to cross. That's why CBP's own data shows this region consistently has some of the lowest numbers of border crossings of any part of the southwestern border. And, you know, the remoteness is why people love it. I mean, when you're up in the sky over these huge mountains and steep canyons, it's beautiful. It looks prehistoric. It's untouched. And that is what people love about this region. Commissioner Scott said yesterday, in fact, he was going to get his own aerial tour of the region, as he's set to meet with local leaders.
PFEIFFER: And, Travis, you've touched on this, this sort of outpouring of, as you said, bipartisan outrage. But give us more of a sense, especially for listeners who haven't been to Big Bend, about why people feel so strongly about this place.
BUBENIK: You know, anyone who ever comes out here even once loves it. I mean, it is beautiful, wide-open country. It is the mythic picture of what Texas is supposed to be, you know (laughter)? It's sometimes called Texas' gift to the nation. And locals just say that these border plans could change this region forever, and, more pressingly, could kill this region's tourism-dependent economy. A lot of the economy here is river trips on the Rio Grande, camping and hiking in the national park. At a protest in the park last week, Jessica Bartko, a local river outfitter whose business depends on tourists, spoke out against these plans.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
JESSICA BARTKO: This is not Texan. This is not American. Our parks belong to the American public. We have entrusted our federal government to protect our parks, not destroy them. What they are doing is actively waging a war against our parks, our public lands, our communities and our livelihoods.
BUBENIK: And Commissioner Scott has said in recent days his agency is, quote, "securing this park to protect its legacy." But, again, locals just say any new border infrastructure out here is an existential threat to their way of life.
PFEIFFER: That is Travis Bubenik with Marfa Public Radio. Travis, thank you for covering this for us.
BUBENIK: You're welcome.

sources.text:
The Trump administration said Monday it is temporarily pausing construction of a contentious border project in Texas’s Big Bend National Park.
Rodney Scott, who leads Customs and Border Protection, is scheduled to visit the site.
Scott said that over the next couple of days, he plans to “listen to local leadership, community members, and stakeholders” as the administration looks to continue protecting the park while addressing “real” national security threats.
The project has drawn fierce bipartisan opposition. Critics say it undermines the area’s pristine environment. They say the region’s rugged and remote terrain already deters illegal immigrants and smugglers.
The Big Bend Sector—responsible for 517 miles or roughly one-quarter of the U.S. Southwest border—is employing a strategy that balances personnel, technology, and infrastructure to secure the border.
It remains unclear whether the brief suspension signals a longer halt.
Local Opposition
Opposition has been especially fierce in Texas near Big Bend National Park and a state park to the west. Customs and Border Protection earlier this year backed off plans for a 30-foot-tall bollard wall through the parks. It has continued with other measures: a new road, lights, miles of barriers meant to stop vehicles, and technology such as fiber optic cables buried under fences.
That approach has drawn ire from Democratic and Republican sheriffs in the region, former national park officials, local residents who depend on the parks for their livelihoods, and some Texas elected officials. Critics say the work will mar the rugged landscape that draws tourists who raft the Rio Grande and take advantage of some of the clearest night skies in the United States.
“We are working to preserve the landscape and protect the access visitors and local residents depend on,” it stated.
Sen. John Cornyn, who lost the Republican primary to the state’s attorney general, wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin about the construction.
“My constituents believe that the 1,000-foot riverbank cliffs and remote Big Bend terrain offers its own source of deterrence for any illegal migrants crossing into the United States,” Cornyn wrote. “The dangerous terrain includes steep mountains, deep canyons, and expansive deserts, which they believe act as a natural barrier that limits large-scale movements.”

sources.news_title: Trump Admin Pauses Big Bend National Park Border Project
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration said Monday it is temporarily stopping construction on a disputed border security project in Texas’ Big Bend National Park, as the head of the agency overseeing the work travels to the area for what officials described as an “on-the-ground evaluation.”
The border project cutting through the national park in South Texas has drawn sharp bipartisan criticism from opponents who warn it could scar one of the country’s most unspoiled landscapes. Critics also contend that Big Bend’s isolated, mountainous terrain already discourages migrants and smugglers. Illegal border crossings in the area have long been lower than in other sectors and have declined even more over the past two years.
“CBP is pausing all construction activity in Big Bend National Park while I visit and conduct a personal, on-the-ground evaluation,” Rodney Scott, the head of Customs and Border Protection, wrote on X. Scott said that over the next couple of days he planned to “listen to local leadership, community members and stakeholders” as the agency weighs what he called “real” national security threats while also protecting the park.
Pause marks a rare concession from Trump administration — but unclear for how long
It was not immediately clear whether the short-term pause could lead to a longer or permanent halt to construction in the area. Still, the move underscored the strength of the bipartisan pushback and marked an unusual concession by the administration on one of President Donald Trump’s central campaign promises, a project officials have moved quickly to advance.
Congress last summer provided the Trump administration with $46 billion to build a border wall stretching from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico. Since then, the administration has pressed ahead aggressively, waiving numerous regulations in an effort to speed construction.
Scott has previously said he expects the first layer of the wall to be completed by the end of next year.
But in Texas, the administration has encountered intense resistance, particularly over construction in and around Big Bend National Park and a state park located to the west.
Earlier this year, Customs and Border Protection retreated from plans to build a 30-foot-tall bollard wall through the parks. Even so, the agency continued pursuing other border security measures, including a new road, lighting, miles of vehicle barriers intended to prevent cars from crossing the border, and technology such as fiber optic cables that would be buried beneath the fencing.
That has sparked opposition from Democratic and Republican sheriffs in the region, former national park officials, local residents who rely on the parks for their livelihood and some Texas elected officials. Critics have said it will scar the rugged landscape that attracts tourists who raft down the Rio Grande River and take advantage of some of the clearest night skies in the U.S. to gaze at stars.
Last week, bulldozers were seen clearing land at the park, sparking even more concern and raising questions from one of the state’s Republican senators.
At the time the bulldozers were seen, the Department of Homeland Security said on X that they were related to “survey and design work.”
Sen. John Cornyn, who lost the Republican primary to the state’s attorney general, wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin over construction concerns.
“My constituents believe that the 1,000-foot riverbank cliffs and remote Big Bend terrain offers its own source of deterrence for any illegal migrants crossing into the United States. The dangerous terrain includes steep mountains, deep canyons, and expansive deserts which they believe act a natural barrier that limits large-scale movements,” Cornyn wrote.
As the wall-building efforts have shifted into high gear this year along the roughly 2,000-mile border, opposition has spiked as well.
The administration has faced criticism from Native American groups saying wall contractors are desecrating religious sites, a small Texas town worried the wall will damage its levee system, and a Catholic archdiocese that says wall construction in the El Paso area mars an important religious site.
Activists praise the pause but say it’s only a first step
Activists who have been rallying opposition to the administration’s plans said they were encouraged by the pause but they would be watching closely to see if CBP makes any significant changes or simply goes back to its previous plans.
Bob Krumenaker was the superintendent of Big Bend National Park from 2018 to 2023 and now chairs the organization “Keep Big Bend Wild,” which aims to preserve the park’s wild nature. He said he was “wary but optimistic” after news of the pause.
“They are paying attention to all of the objections that have been raised across the political spectrum,” he said.
But Krumenaker said it’s unlikely that CBP is going to entirely abandon all its plans in the region. Krumenaker said he and others would be watching to see whether the equipment like the bulldozers is removed from the park, the agency outlines a clear plan going forward and it repairs any damage already done.
“Let’s hope they significantly modify their plans in response to what they hear, and make it transparent,” he said.
Another group, which sued Homeland Security over its decision to broadly waive regulations to speed up construction projects in the Big Bend region, called the announcement “welcome news” but warned that construction could resume “at any moment.”
“This temporary pause proves how much non-partisan public pressure is mounting in West Texas and across America to stop the irreversible destruction unfolding in this crown jewel national park,” said Laiken Jordahl with the Center for Biological Diversity.
“We’re not resting until these contracts are canceled, these workers are sent packing, the waivers are rescinded and every wall plan for the greater Big Bend region is scrapped for good.”

sources.news_title: CBP Pauses Border Security Projects in Big Bend National Park Amid Public Outcry
sources.text:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott announced his agency put a temporary halt to ongoing infrastructure projects underway at Big Bend National Park in West Texas. Scott announced on Monday on the social media platform X that the projects would be paused while he meets with local stakeholders and law enforcement this week.
As reported by Breitbart Texas, the projects have come under scrutiny from politicians on both sides of the aisle. Senator John Cornyn (R-TX) recently added his voice to those of local politicians and James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in the 2026 U.S. Senate election in Texas, in opposing border security enhancements in Big Bend National Park. In a letter addressed to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin dated August 7, Cornyn echoed constituents’ belief that dangerous terrain in the region acts as a “natural barrier that limits large-scale movements.”
In the letter, Cornyn urges Secretary Mullin to consider meeting with stakeholders to reconsider proposed border security infrastructure projects in the region and pause construction until concerns have been addressed. Cornyn’s intervention in the matter was met with quick praise by Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico.
The pause comes after a protest at the park earlier in August, organized by the Center for Biological Diversity. The event was attended by environmental activists and opponents of border security from the border region and the Austin, Texas, area. The organization opposes border infrastructure projects from California to Texas on the grounds they threaten the ecology and sites of cultural importance along the border.
On Monday, Texas Governor Greg Abbott credited his outreach with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin for influencing the decision to pause the infrastructure projects within the park. At an unrelated press event in Waco, Texas, Abbott declared, “He committed to me they will not be building a wall or a fence in Big Bend National Park.” Abbott believes that technology could replace physical infrastructure in this region.
The installation of physical barriers within the state has also proven unpopular with ranchers outside the park. The projects have been met with skepticism by many private landowners, many of whom hold large tracts of land and are wary of losing access to parts of their property due to construction of border barriers. The ranchers also worry about impacts to livestock and hunting activities caused by increased federal presence on their property.
A report by the Texas Tribune showed that as many as a third of landowners approached by the state in 2024 refused to allow Abbott to build a border wall on their properties. Mike Novak, Executive Director of the Texas Facilities Commission overseeing the Texas border wall projects, called opposition to border wall construction the most daunting hurdle to completing the border wall, according to a Texas Tribune report.
Commissioner Scott did not indicate how long the pause would last or how much it would cost taxpayers, who must continue to fund the effort while work sits idle. In an exclusive report by Breitbart Texas, the 2021 border wall pause initiated by the Biden Administration was reported to have cost taxpayers $6 million per day as equipment and work crews sat idle for months until the projects were finally canceled in their entirety.
In this case, the pause could cost significantly less, specifically for the construction of border security projects within Big Bend National Park. According to federal contract regulations, contractors must immediately stop work, implement “make safe” activities, and take steps to mitigate costs during any pause in a federal project.
CBP has indicated that the Big Bend National Park projects will involve only the construction of one new access road, the improvement of existing roads, the installation of detection technology, and the placement of vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations.
According to CBP, the work will not involve constructing a 30-foot border wall in the park. Despite this, liberal activists allege the projects will destroy the park. The pause was quickly celebrated by Congressman Greg Casar (D-TX), who announced the victory on social media platform X, saying, “The public outcry is working. Keep up the pressure until they fully abandon the plan to wreck Big Bend for no reason other than to make contractors money. Law enforcement, conservationists, Democrats, Republicans, Texans all agree: leave Big Bend alone.” Congressman Casar has frequently criticized the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement posture and has called for ICE to be completely abolished.
According to CBP, the agency sought public input on the projects from June to July 2026 as they relate to “potential impacts to the environment, culture, and commerce, including socioeconomic impacts, and quality of life.” The comment period was closed on July 13, 2026. Commissioner Scott did not indicate why additional outreach was needed.
Randy Clark is a 32-year veteran of the United States Border Patrol. Before his retirement, he served as the Division Chief for Law Enforcement Operations, directing operations for nine Border Patrol Stations within the Del Rio, Texas, Sector. Follow him on X (formerly Twitter) @RandyClarkBBTX.

Sierra Club Demands Permanent Halt to Trump’s Big Bend Construction
|  | 
|  | 
| CBP pauses work pending an on-site review after bulldozers tear through land near Santa Elena Canyon  AUSTIN, Texas — Following widespread bipartisan outrage, Donald Trump’s U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott announced Monday that the agency is temporarily pausing all construction activity in Big Bend National Park as he visits the site this week. Scott did not say how long the pause would last or commit to canceling the project.  The announcement follows vast bipartisan opposition after contractors used heavy machinery to clear native vegetation and disturb wildlife near the mouth of Santa Elena Canyon. The National Park Service closed part of the area to the public on Aug. 12 because of large-scale construction work. The construction project threatens critical wildlife habitat, recommended wilderness landscapes, and cultural and historic areas.  In response, Jackie Feinberg, manager of the Sierra Club’s Lands Conservation campaign released the following statement: “Big Bend should never have been bulldozed for a destructive border project, and the Trump administration must make this pause permanent and repair the damage already done. Anything less than a full withdrawal is unacceptable for the millions of Americans across the country who love and cherish our national parks and public lands. The Sierra Club will keep fighting until this project is permanently rescinded. We call on Congress to act to defend Big Bend and ensure that our shared lands and waters nationwide are protected for generations to come.”  In response Dave Cortez, director of the Sierra Club Lone Star Chapter released the following statement: “West Texas will not stand by while these irreplaceable landscapes remain at risk. This pause is a step in the right direction, but the threat has not passed. While we call on Texans of all political stripes to continue to press Governor Abbott to defend Big Bend, we need every American who cherishes our public lands to continue to contact their members of Congress and encourage them to abandon every plan that puts Big Bend in harm’s way.”   About the Sierra Club The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. In addition to protecting every person’s right to get outdoors and access the healing power of nature, the Sierra Club works to promote clean energy, safeguard the health of our communities, protect wildlife, and preserve our remaining wild places through grassroots activism, public education, lobbying, and legal action. sources.news_title: Trump admin halts border wall construction amid concerns over Big Bend
sources.text:
The Trump administration has halted construction activity tied to a controversial border-security project in Texas' Big Bend National Park after days of mounting criticism from environmental groups, tribal advocates, local residents and lawmakers.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Commissioner Rodney Scott announced Monday that all construction activity in the park would be paused while he conducts a personal review of the project and meets with local stakeholders.
"Last night, I put a pause on all activity in that park as far as construction goes until I can get down there and do a personal evaluation, talk to some stakeholders, talk to local law enforcement in that area," Scott said in a video posted to X. "More to follow this week."
Mike Davidson, who works as a tour guide in Big Bend, told Newsweek on Monday: "There's been very little opportunity for public input so this seems promising. But I am not holding my breath for any real changes. Meanwhile caravans of vehicles and machinery have been photographed en route to staging areas."
The decision follows growing controversy over work taking place inside one of America's most iconic national parks, where critics have warned that planned roads, barriers and surveillance infrastructure could damage sensitive desert landscapes, wildlife habitat and culturally significant sites.
"While the Big Bend business community welcomes any pause in construction, our region's entire tourism economy remains at risk until the project is cancelled outright," Sara Ryza, of the Big Bend Tourism Alliance, told Newsweek Monday.
"In addition to the destruction of our national park with bulldozed roads and planned vehicle barriers, even in the remotest stretches of the park headed toward Mariscal Mountain, there are camps in communities like Terlingua and just north of the park entrance. Who wants to vacation in a construction zone? And what will Big Bend National Park look like when they're done?"
Newsweek reached out on Monday to CBP.
Why It Matters
Big Bend spans more than 800,000 acres along the U.S.-Mexico border and is widely regarded as one of the country's most remote and ecologically significant protected areas.
The dispute has become a high-profile test of the Trump administration's effort to expand border-security infrastructure while facing opposition from conservation groups, tribal organizations, tourism advocates and some elected officials. The controversy has also drawn national attention after images of bulldozers and other heavy equipment operating inside the park circulated online and fueled concerns about the project's environmental impact.
The pause comes as tribal and environmental groups pursue legal action seeking to stop the work and as questions persist about how far the government intends to go with planned construction in the region.
What Was Being Built?
The debate over Big Bend has often been described as a fight over President Donald Trump's border wall agenda, but administration officials maintain they are not building a traditional border wall through the national park.
In a statement provided to Newsweek last week, Scott said CBP was constructing "one new access road," improving existing roads, installing detection technology and placing vehicle barriers in strategic locations.
"We are not building a 30-foot wall or stadium lighting through Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, or the Black Gap Wildlife Management Area," Scott said.
The commissioner argued that the improvements would help Border Patrol agents detect illegal crossings, respond more quickly in emergencies and secure a remote section of the southern border.
Federal officials have repeatedly said the work is part of a broader border-security strategy that extends well beyond the national park itself.
Bryan Devonshire, the owner and founder of Astro Mucho, a stargazing business in Terlingua, told Newsweek, "I feel like I just finished a round of non-consensual torture. I am grateful that the pain has stopped. I'm happy that the habitat gets to rest for at least one day and the native graves are stilled from the vibrations of heavy machinery."
Why Critics Are Alarmed
The Trump administration's assurances have not eased concerns among environmental groups and local advocates.
Opponents argue that even road construction and vehicle barriers could fundamentally alter portions of the park's landscape. Critics have pointed to Mariscal Mountain, a rugged limestone ridge overlooking the Rio Grande, as one of the most controversial elements of the project.
Earlier this month, the Center for Biological Diversity warned that road construction across the mountain could require extensive blasting because of the challenging terrain. The group described the work as a threat to one of Texas' most treasured natural areas.
Lawmakers have also raised questions about whether construction could damage sensitive ecosystems, archaeological resources and wildlife habitat.
Former Big Bend wildlife biologist Raymond Skiles said in a July Facebook post that Mariscal Canyon has hosted as many as three nesting pairs of peregrine falcons annually, describing it as "likely Texas' most densely populated Peregrine nesting area" and noting that the birds are highly sensitive to disturbance near their cliffside nesting sites.
The growing backlash has united an unusual coalition that includes environmental advocates, local tourism interests, former National Park Service officials, tribal groups and some Texas elected leaders.
Lawsuit Seeks to Stop Project
The controversy intensified Friday when The People of La Junta for Preservation, a nonprofit associated with members of the Lipan Apache community, and Far Flung Outdoor Center filed a federal lawsuit seeking to halt the project. The suit was also brought by Christina Hernandez, the preservation group's founder and director, and Andrew Austin, whom the complaint describes as a practitioner of Native religion and a lineal descendant of the Lipan Apache people.
The plaintiffs allege that planned construction involving roads, barriers, excavation, lighting, cameras, sensors and related infrastructure threatens archaeological resources, ancestral landscapes, traditional-use areas and places of cultural and potentially religious significance.
The complaint argues that damage to those resources could not be undone, stating that "once an archaeological site is excavated by heavy machinery, once the physical context of artifacts is destroyed, or once a sacred or culturally significant landscape is permanently altered, the injury is irreparable."
The lawsuit also alleges that the project could interfere with Indigenous religious practices tied to the Rio Grande and the broader Big Bend landscape, including prayer, gathering ceremonial materials, access to burial places and other traditional religious observances.
Far Flung, a Terlingua-based outdoor recreation business, alleges that roads, barriers, lighting and other infrastructure could impair the visitor experience and hurt tourism demand in a region that depends heavily on recreation and park visitation.
The legal challenge is the latest obstacle facing the border initiative and increases pressure on federal officials to provide more details about what they intend to build and where.
Border Security Versus Conservation
Supporters of the project say the enhancements are necessary because criminal organizations can shift routes and exploit vulnerable stretches of the border.
The administration has pointed to migrant encounters, drug seizures and other enforcement activity in the Big Bend Sector as justification for additional infrastructure. Scott has argued that securing the region is essential even if migration patterns change in the future.
Critics, however, note that unlawful crossings in the sector have fallen sharply during Trump's second term.
CBP data shows Border Patrol recorded 148 migrant encounters in the Big Bend Sector in June 2026, down from 412 in June 2023. During the first nine months of fiscal year 2026, authorities recorded 1,509 encounters compared with 10,291 during the same period in fiscal year 2023, an 85 percent decline.
Terrell County Sheriff Thaddeus Cleveland welcomed Scott's decision to visit the region, saying he had encouraged the commissioner to see the area firsthand for months because he believed the original proposal was flawed.
"I'm glad Commissioner Scott is finally coming out to the Big Bend," Cleveland told Newsweek on Monday. "I've been encouraging him to visit for months because I've believed from the first announcement that the original plan was flawed."
Cleveland, who said he previously worked with Scott as a Border Patrol agent and later served in Scott's office in Washington, D.C., praised the commissioner for scaling back what Cleveland described as an earlier proposal that would have placed a 30-foot barrier across the entire Big Bend Sector. He said Scott had told him he would personally evaluate areas around Big Bend National Park and Big Bend Ranch State Park before deciding how to proceed.
Still, Cleveland questioned the need for a road near Mariscal Canyon, arguing that the terrain itself makes the area an unlikely route for smuggling activity.
"I do not believe the road being constructed near Mariscal Canyon is warranted," Cleveland said. "This is a 1,500-foot vertical cliff above the Rio Grande River. This area isn't used by smugglers and if it was, we could certainly deploy technology on the ground and in the air to protect it."
He added that the road would be unlikely to see substantial use because of the area's remoteness and limited manpower assigned to the national park.
What Happens Next
Scott's announcement does not mean the project has been canceled. Instead, it signals that federal officials are temporarily stepping back while the CBP commissioner evaluates conditions on the ground and hears directly from local leaders, law enforcement officials and other stakeholders.
The commissioner indicated additional information could be released later this week following his visit.
For now, construction activity inside Big Bend National Park has been put on hold, leaving the future of one of the Trump administration's most closely watched border-security projects uncertain as legal, environmental and political questions continue to mount.
"I hope this is actually the beginning of communication with CBP. I hope that reason can find a way to permanently stop this destruction," Devonshire said. "But as long as the equipment and crews remain in Big Bend, I am bound in my dungeon, wondering when the pain will resume."
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins.

Crews had begun clearing land in the park earlier this month for roads and border security infrastructure, prompting protests and lawsuits seeking to halt the work.

President Donald Trump, a Republican, has touted building or reinforcing barriers along the U.S.-Mexico border as part of his anti-immigration policies. Republicans control all three branches of government in Texas.

“Last night, I put a pause on all activity in that park as far as construction goes till I can get down there and do a personal evaluation, talk to some stakeholders, talk to some local law enforcement in that area,” Scott said in a video posted on X.
The project has received bipartisan opposition from critics who argue the construction would damage the ecosystem and animals inside the national park.
What is the project?
In 2025, Congress approved $46 billion to build a border wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico. Since then, the administration has waived environmental regulations to accelerate the project.
In June, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote that the administration was waiving “certain laws, regulations, and other legal requirements” to ensure “expeditious construction of barriers and roads” on the U.S.-Mexico border.
Contractors began bulldozing parts of the national park for the project last week, Straight Arrow reported.
CBP originally said it planned to build a 30-foot border wall through the parks but has since backed off. Instead, the agency said the project would include a new road, lights, vehicle barriers and infrastructure like fiber-optic cable, the AP reported.
On Monday, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott told reporters that Mullin assured him that “they will not be building a wall or a fence in Big Bend National Park.”
Bipartisan criticism in Big Bend
The project has drawn criticism from multiple groups, including the Texas Chapter of Backcountry Hunters & Anglers. In March, the group issued a statement saying it has “significant concerns” about the border wall, and “the subsequent impacts to our North American heritage of hunting and fishing in a natural setting.”
“It would block popular hiking trails, and it would permanently scar the beautiful Santa Elena and Boquillas Canyons,” BHA added. “It would close off access to nearly 200 miles of the Rio Grande for American paddlers, river guides, anglers, land stewards, and sightseers — from Big Bend National Park to Amistad National Wildlife Refuge.”
But the project also prompted lawmakers close to Trump to express their concerns. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, wrote last week to Mullin, saying Big Bend’s terrain creates its own natural obstacles to those trying to cross the border illegally.
“My constituents believe that the 1,000-foot riverbank cliffs and remote Big Bend terrain offers its own source of deterrence for any illegal migrants crossing into the United States,” Cornyn wrote. “The dangerous terrain includes steep mountains, deep canyons, and expansive deserts which they believe act a natural barrier that limits large-scale movements.”
Does the US need a wall in Big Bend?
The Big Bend region contains about 517 miles of the nearly 2,000 miles of the total southern border. Despite this, the area sees few illegal crossings.
In 2023, CBP said the U.S. saw just under 2.5 million total illegal border crossings along the southern border, but the Big Bend region accounted for just over 11,000 of those. That number has also decreased since Trump returned to office. In 2025, the Big Bend area saw just under 3,100 illegal border crossings.
The Trump administration’s border wall project has also received criticism from residents in other areas of the country. In May, people in Arizona complained that the project damaged part of a Native American site that scientists believe is at least 1,000 years old.
Then in June, the Tohono O’odham Nation filed a lawsuit alleging the project would “illegally violate the Nation’s rights as a sovereign tribe.”
The tribe said it has previously approved the construction for on-reservation border vehicle barriers, patrol roads, surveillance towers and Border Patrol operating bases. But tribal leaders made it clear that it would not support border wall construction on their lands.
“We have tried to work with the Department on the border wall issue, but it insists on rushing forward with construction,” Tohono O’odham Nation Chairman Verlon Jose said. “We have been left with no other choice but to file suit to protect our land, our culture, and our rights.”

U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott said Monday he was "pausing all construction activity" in Big Bend National Park ahead of a visit to the area this week.
The Trump administration has faced a growing public outcry in recent days over images of bulldozers and other heavy machinery clearing land inside the sprawling West Texas park in pursuit of its plan to build new "patrol roads" across the park and install 17 miles of steel vehicle barriers.
In a video posted to social media, Scott said he had ordered the construction paused Sunday night, and that he was en route to the park for a "personal evaluation" and talk to local law enforcement and other stakeholders. Scott later indicated in a social media post that he would be flying over the area.
"We know the current and predictable national security threats and they are real," Scott said in a statement accompanying the video. "Now over the next couple of days, I will join a small team to evaluate the terrain and listen to local leadership, community members and stakeholders to ensure that we secure our borders while simultaneously protecting BBNP for generations to come."
A CBP spokesperson did not immediately answer questions about the planned visit.
Scott's visit comes just days after he had initially defended the construction work in the park, describing it as "survey and design work" and reiterating that CBP was not seeking to build a 30-foot steel border wall.
For months, locals and activists opposed to the work have insisted they remain concerned about current plans for the park, which would amount to a widespread construction project unconstrained by federal regulations. The Trump administration in June waived many environmental laws that would typically apply to such construction in a national park. Southwest Valley Constructors, a subsidiary of Nebraska-based construction giant Kiewet, was awarded a $1.7 billion contract in May for the Big Bend National Park project.
Activists have continued in recent days to document scenes of the construction, showing bulldozers and other heavy equipment clearing land through multiple parts of the park, from the popular Santa Elena Canyon scenic viewpoint along the Rio Grande to the extremely remote Mariscal Mountain area, one of the park's most isolated and rugged regions.
"This temporary pause proves how much non-partisan public pressure is mounting in West Texas and across America to stop the irreversible destruction unfolding in this crown jewel national park," said Laiken Jordahl, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity, which is among the entities that have sued the Trump administration over its Big Bend area border plans.
Still, Jordahl warned that "construction at Big Bend is likely to resume at any moment."
"We're not resting until these contracts are canceled, these workers are sent packing, the waivers are rescinded and every wall plan for the greater Big Bend region is scrapped for good," he said.
On Monday morning, Marfa Public Radio reporters took a flight over Big Bend National Park and did not see active construction activity underway at either the Santa Elena Canyon area or Mariscal Mountain. Near Mariscal, the reporters saw heavy machinery stationed near the start of what appeared to be a new path off an existing road — one activists had captured videos of crews building over the weekend.
The Trump administration is meanwhile facing multiple lawsuits over both its border plans in Big Big Bend National Park and its ongoing pursuit of a 30-foot steel border wall in the greater Big Bend region, from Hudspeth to Presidio counties.
In the most recent case, a local indigenous group asked a federal judge over the weekend for a temporary block on construction. There's no clear timeline for when the judge in that case might rule on the request.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott has paused border construction in Big Bend National Park while he conducts an on-site review following bipartisan, local and environmental opposition to the project.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
U.S. Customs and Border Protection has temporarily stopped construction activity in Big Bend National Park as Commissioner Rodney Scott prepares to personally review the project and meet with local officials and other stakeholders.
Scott announced the pause Monday after opposition grew over planned border-security work in the remote West Texas park, including concerns from Republican officials, residents, businesses, environmental groups and law enforcement.
“I put a pause on all activity in that park, as far as construction goes, until I can get down there and do a personal evaluation, talk to some stakeholders, talk to some local law enforcement in that area,” Scott said in a video posted on X. “More to follow this week.”
In a separate statement, Scott said he and a small team would travel to the area to assess the project directly.
He said the group will “evaluate the terrain and listen to local leadership, community members and stakeholders to ensure that we secure our borders while simultaneously protecting BBNP for generations to come.”
The decision came after bulldozers arrived at Big Bend National Park for work CBP described as surveying and design activity.
It was not immediately clear how long construction would remain paused or whether Scott’s review could result in changes to the project’s scope.
CBP has sought to counter claims that the project would involve a conventional large-scale border wall through the park.
The agency said last week that it does not intend to construct a 30-foot wall or install stadium-style lighting inside Big Bend National Park.
Instead, CBP said its plans call for vehicle barriers, patrol and access roads, cameras, sensors and other detection systems while preserving visitor access.
“These improvements will help our agents detect illegal crossings, respond faster, and assist visitors in danger,” Scott said. “As we strengthen the border across the Southwest, we will not leave Big Bend as an opening for cartels to exploit by shifting their routes and tactics.”
The broader Big Bend project is backed by a $1.7 billion contract awarded May 11.
The contract covers 17 miles of vehicle barriers and patrol roads, along with 205 miles of what CBP describes as “system attributes,” which combine roads with surveillance and detection technology throughout the region.
Opponents argue the unique geography of Big Bend already creates a formidable natural barrier.
The area is marked by cliffs, mountains and rugged desert terrain, conditions critics say make illegal crossings difficult without extensive new construction.
They have also warned that development could damage wildlife habitat, alter scenic areas and hurt an economy that relies heavily on visitors drawn to the park’s largely undeveloped landscape.
The Big Bend Sector spans 517 miles of the southern border, yet it recorded the fewest apprehensions among the Border Patrol’s nine southern border sectors during fiscal 2025.
The sector accounted for 1.3% of more than 237,000 apprehensions recorded along the U.S.-Mexico border that year.
Those figures have contributed to arguments from critics who question whether the scale of the proposed infrastructure is necessary in the region.
Opposition has crossed party lines.
Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, urged Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to stop construction pending consultations with local communities.
In an Aug. 7 letter, Cornyn asked the department to ensure that security improvements take into account both the park’s landscape and its importance to the local economy.
Texas Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham, also a Republican, raised a separate objection after her office said federal contractors had carried out unauthorized work on state-managed property in Presidio County.
On July 31, Buckingham sent cease-and-desist letters to CBP and Barnard Construction, alleging that a contractor illegally cleared more than a mile of state-managed land.
She also demanded that the affected property be restored.
Federal officials had previously taken steps to accelerate construction by waiving a range of environmental and preservation requirements.
In February, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem invoked federal waiver authority to set aside more than two dozen environmental and historic preservation laws for planned barriers and roads in the Big Bend Sector.
A separate waiver issued in May covered additional projects in the region.
Scott’s decision does not cancel the project or the underlying contract.
Instead, construction inside the park will remain paused while he reviews conditions firsthand and speaks with local officials, law enforcement, residents and other stakeholders.
The commissioner said that review will guide the agency’s next steps as CBP seeks to balance its border-security plans with concerns about protecting Big Bend National Park and the surrounding communities.

(The Center Square) – U.S. Customs and Border Protection Chief Rodney Scott said he paused all construction activity in Big Bend National Park and arrived in Texas on Monday to meet with Texas officials and stakeholders in person. He said he’s meeting with “a small team to evaluate the terrain and listen to local leadership, community members and stakeholders to ensure that we secure our borders while simultaneously protecting BBNP.”
He made the announcement after extensive pressure from Texas state lawmakers, sheriffs, and business owners and after Texans have filed multiple lawsuits against CBP.
Scott succumbed to pressure after a former colleague who served with him in Border Patrol, now Terrell County Sheriff, Thad Cleveland, called on him to halt construction. Cleveland invited Scott to the area to learn what infrastructure should be installed based on “the terrain, operational effectiveness, and the realities on the ground.” Cleveland has advocated for a “virtual wall,” using radar, Anduril Autonomous Surveillance Towers, thermal cameras and other technology, The Center Square reported.
Scott’s announcement came after U.S. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, called on him and others to listen to Texans, The Center Square reported. Cornyn raised concerns about the waivers signed by former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and current secretary Markwayne Mullin authorizing destruction of Native American property, historical Texas structures and west Texas land that has existed untouched for centuries.
Under Scott, Texans received notices that DHS would use imminent domain to take their land to build border wall barriers if they didn’t agree to terms, The Center Square reported.
The Texas General Land Office has also gotten involved, ordering CBP to stop illegally destroying state land, or it would sue, The Center Square reported. State Sen. Roland Gutierrez, D-El Paso, has also sued, retaining well-known Houston attorney, Dick DeGuerin.
Thousands of Texans have called on Congress to halt construction in Big Bend, pointing to less than one percent of illegal crossings occurring there and natural 1,500-foot-high barriers providing a deterrent. U.S. Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, said a border wall wasn’t needed in the park and that high-ranking officials told him CBP was “only putting in a caliche road with buried cables for tech monitoring plus vehicle barriers consistent with other national parks to prevent vehicles from going places they should not, and nothing more.”
“Congress – and specifically the Texas delegation – must get a full briefing on this issue from the administration,” he added.
Scott’s arrival in Texas comes after a bipartisan coalition of state lawmakers called on Gov. Greg Abbott to intervene to no avail. The latest request was led by Democrat state Rep. Eddie Morales, Jr., who said, “God has blessed this region with a natural border wall – there is simply no need to spend upwards of $7 billion on shady no-bid contracts on a sector that saw less than ~1% of crossings. Texas does not, and should not, bend the knee to the will of the federal government. Texas leaders swore an oath to protect our state, our land, and our communities – it is imperative that oath is upheld to protect this region for future generations of Texans to cherish.”
State Rep. Drew Darby, a Republican who signed the letter, said, “we have a duty to speak up when federal action threatens our land and our communities. This is not a Democrat or Republican issue; it is a Texan issue. We have an obligation to secure our border, but Big Bend's rugged, unforgiving terrain already serves as a natural, God-given barrier that deters illegal crossings. The border crossing data already confirms this. … We owe it to future generations of Texans to protect Big Bend, and to ensure the hunting, ranching, and agribusiness operations that sustain this region can continue unimpeded.”
Former Texas House Speaker Dade Phelan, R-Beaumont, criticized the Trump administration for approving no bid contracts, saying, “The standard federal competitive bid process was waived under Section 102(c) of the IIRIRA. We know how that works out. #ReflectionPool. I agree with Morales but rarely sign letters. We can secure this area through technology and manpower.”
Contractors have been awarded billions in no bid contracts to build border barriers, including those who donated to the president and have criminal histories, The Center Square reported.
In response to ongoing bipartisan public outrage, DHS claimed, “The mainstream media is fear mongering about our work at Big Bend. Here’s what’s actually happening: CBP is building ONE new access road, improving existing roads, installing detection technology, and placing vehicle barriers in limited, strategic locations. What people are seeing is survey and design work — NOT construction of a wall or stadium lighting through” Big Bend.
Center for Biological Diversity’s Laiken Jordahl, who is also suing the administration, posted drone footage of contractors bulldozing into Big Bend’s Mariscal Mountain in just the last two days, saying DHS was “lying.”
Abbott has remained silent on the issue and his office has not responded to requests for comment. Multiple lawmakers have called on Abbott to act and argue the attorney general should sue the federal government to stop construction but won’t.
Jordahl added that Abbott will “forever be remembered as the one who let the feds tread all over [Texas’] sovereignty and natural heritage” and his “silence is a rubberstamp on this destruction.”

A top Trump administration official said Monday that construction on a controversial border security project at Big Bend National Park had been paused after months of outrage from local residents and advocacy organizations.
Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott confirmed in a post on X that he had halted all construction activity in the park, at least temporarily, as of Sunday night. He also confirmed that he was en route to the park to meet with “stakeholders and local law enforcement in the area.”
NOTUS first reported Scott’s plans to travel to the Big Bend region on Friday.
The visit comes after months of outcry from nearby residents, advocacy groups, lawmakers and local law enforcement. Earlier this year, CBP announced plans for a “smart wall” that included 30-foot physical walls through some of the national park. The plans faced swift backlash, leading the agency to announce that its plans would not include the massive barriers, but would instead be made up of patrol roads, surveillance technology and vehicle barriers.
Trending
Concerns escalated earlier this summer when Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin waived a handful of environmental and historical preservation laws, including some aimed at protecting drinking water and endangered species, and a statute requiring federal agencies to return any Native American remains and sacred objects to affiliated tribes.
CBP is pausing all construction activity in Big Bend National Park while I visit and conduct a personal, on-the-ground evaluation.
CBP is firmly committed to protecting America,  and that includes our national treasures like Big Bend National Park (BBNP). We know the current and… pic.twitter.com/UkmzvTluwH
Tensions again rose when bulldozers were seen clearing land in the national park earlier this month.
The Big Bend Sector has some of the lowest rates of illegal border crossings, particularly within the park. The area has 1,000-foot cliffs in various places, which advocates and local officials say are natural barriers.
“We are working to preserve the landscape and protect the access visitors and local businesses depend on,” a CBP spokesperson wrote in a statement to NOTUS. “We are currently evaluating technology options to meet President Trump’s mission of zero illegal border crossings while strengthening the most secure border in American history in highly remote and hard-to-access areas.”
It is unclear how long Scott plans to visit the region, or what will happen to the multimillion- dollar contracts that the administration has already awarded for work in the Big Bend region.
The area falls within Texas’ 23rd Congressional District, which has been sitting vacant since Republican Rep. Tony Gonzales resigned in April after admitting to having an affair with a staffer who later died by suicide.
In the months since, various Democrat lawmakers have sent letters to Mullin over their concerns for the park, including multiple letters led by Rep. Lloyd Doggett of Texas, urging the administration to reconsider its plans. On Aug. 7, Republican Sen. John Cornyn sent a letter to Mullin urging the administration to coordinate and communicate with stakeholders in the region before moving forward with its plans, becoming the highest-ranking Republican to do so.

Trump pauses Big Bend border project amid bipartisan backlash in Texas
The Trump administration has paused border construction in Big Bend National Park pending a site review by CBP chief Rodney Scott. The halt follows bipartisan criticism that the project could damage the park despite relatively low crossings in the area.
The Trump administration has temporarily paused construction of a disputed border project in Texas' Big Bend National Park, with the head of US Customs and Border Protection set to visit the area for an on-the-ground review. The move comes after strong bipartisan opposition from critics who say the work is damaging the park's environment, even as border crossings in the area have historically been lower than in other regions and have fallen further over the past two years.
It is not yet clear whether the pause will lead to a longer halt in construction, but it marks a rare step back by the administration on one of President Donald Trump's signature promises. Congress gave the administration USD 46 billion last summer to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico, and officials have been pushing ahead while waiving several regulations to speed up the work.
Rodney Scott, who heads Customs and Border Protection, said on X: "CBP is pausing all construction activity in Big Bend National Park while I visit and conduct a personal, on-the-ground evaluation." He added that over the next couple of days, he would "listen to local leadership, community members and stakeholders" to address what he described as "real" national security threats while protecting the park.
Scott has said he expects the first layer of the wall to be built by the end of next year. But the administration has faced especially strong resistance in Texas, particularly over construction in and near Big Bend National Park and a state park to the west.
Earlier this year, Customs and Border Protection dropped plans for a 30-foot-tall bollard wall through the parks, but it continued with other border measures. These include a new road, lights, miles of barriers meant to stop vehicles crossing the border, and technology such as fibre optic cables to be buried under the fences.
The continuing work has drawn opposition from Democratic and Republican sheriffs in the region, former national park officials, local residents who depend on the parks for their livelihood, and some Texas elected representatives. Critics say the project will scar the rugged landscape that draws tourists to raft on the Rio Grande River and to see some of the clearest night skies in the US.
Last week, bulldozers were seen clearing land in the park, leading to fresh concern and questions from one of the state's Republican senators. Senator John Cornyn, who lost the Republican primary to the state's attorney general, wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin over the construction. Cornyn wrote: "My constituents believe that the 1,000-foot riverbank cliffs and remote Big Bend terrain offers its own source of deterrence for any illegal migrants crossing into the United States. The dangerous terrain includes steep mountains, deep canyons, and expansive deserts which they believe act as a natural barrier that limits large-scale movements."
For now, construction in Big Bend National Park has been put on hold while Scott reviews the project and meets local stakeholders, after growing opposition to border work in and around the park.

US pauses construction of border project in Texas national park
Houston (AFP) – President Donald Trump's administration said Monday it had paused construction on a $1.7 billion border project at Big Bend National Park in Texas that has faced fierce local opposition across party lines.
Issued on: Modified:
The Department of Homeland Security plans to build vehicle barriers, patrol roads, lighting and detection technology across the park, known for its spectacular views and rich biodiversity, including hundreds of bird species, bobcats and black bears.
Bulldozers broke ground earlier this month on the public lands that blend desert, river and mountain ecosystems and are home to the famed Santa Elena Canyon.
An official map for the project shows a "technology and patrol road" would cross rugged territory -- including the Mariscal Mountain -- which critics say would require extensive dynamite blasting.
"Last night, I put a pause on all activity in that park as far as construction goes, until I get down there and do a personal evaluation," Customs and Border Protection Commissioner Rodney Scott said in a short video posted Monday on X, adding he would talk with local stakeholders and that more updates would come this week.
The Trump administration has waived dozens of environmental laws to greenlight the project, which was awarded through a non-competitive process as part of the president's broader push to build an immense border wall with Mexico.
Residents, officials opposed
There has been a bipartisan backlash from residents and local officials, including all 14 Texas border county judges, who signed an open letter saying they supported border security but wanted more "practical solutions."
According to CBP's data, there are relatively few migrant apprehensions in the Big Bend Sector -- 9,624 between January 2024 and July 2026, compared to 23,080 in the Swanton Sector of the US-Canada border over the same period.
Jake Knight, executive director of the Big Bend Protection Alliance, gestured to the rugged borderlands behind him, telling AFP: "It's quite literally impossible to traverse, whether on foot or in a vehicle, from the other side into this area. Furthermore, this is not the will of the people of this region."
"These are some concerned locals who are really worried about this Big Bend border barrier project," said Bernadette Devine, a 63-year-old teacher, during a protest.
"There's a no-bid contract for $1.7 billion in our national park. And that's an awful lot of money to spend. So we know that they will destroy things. They're already in there right now."
The nonprofit Center for Biological Diversity has sued the government to block the project, alleging the waivers violated the Constitution, and plans to file for an emergency injunction on Monday.
"And while it's certainly welcome news that the bulldozers aren't carving in the national park today, it is very likely that the pause will be lifted, we're not considering this this a victory yet."

Autoridades federales detienen polémicos trabajos de seguridad fronteriza dentro del Parque Nacional Big Bend
Por Ashley Killough y Ed Lavandera, CNN
Todas las obras de seguridad fronteriza en el Parque Nacional Big Bend quedan suspendidas temporalmente, anunció el lunes Rodney Scott, comisionado de la Oficina de Aduanas y Protección Fronteriza de EE.UU. (CBP, por sus siglas en inglés).
Scott dijo en un video publicado en X que aterrizó en Texas y se dirigía a visitar el parque y hablar con las fuerzas del orden locales y otras partes interesadas.
“Anoche ordené suspender toda actividad de construcción en ese parque hasta que pueda llegar allí y hacer una evaluación personal”, dijo en el video.
La medida de Scott se produjo después de que CNN y otros medios informaran sobre el uso de maquinaria pesada por parte del Gobierno durante la última semana para arrasar y excavar partes del parque nacional con el fin de construir caminos de patrullaje y barreras para vehículos. Las obras generaron protestas dentro y en los alrededores del parque nacional, y negocios locales rechazaron a contratistas federales que trabajan en el proyecto. Un grupo bipartidista de alguaciles locales también se ha pronunciado públicamente este año contra los planes de la CBP.
Esos planes incluyen un proyecto más amplio fuera del parque nacional para instalar una extensa infraestructura de seguridad fronteriza a lo largo del río Grande, en la remota región de Texas. Esta zona, denominada “Sector Big Bend” por la CBP, abarca una cuarta parte de la frontera entre EE.UU. y México, pero registra solo cerca del 1 % de las detenciones fronterizas, en parte debido al terreno accidentado de la región.
Los planes actuales de la CBP para la región de Big Bend incluyen la construcción de 282 kilómetros de muro de bolardos de acero de 9 metros de altura a lo largo del río Grande, en zonas al oeste del parque nacional. La agencia no planea construir un muro tradicional de este tipo dentro del parque nacional ni del parque estatal, pero comenzó a despejar terrenos para construir 322 kilómetros de caminos de patrullaje y 27 kilómetros de barreras para vehículos en lugares específicos, informó la agencia la semana pasada. El proyecto de Big Bend también contempla la construcción de 266 kilómetros de barreras para vehículos en zonas al este del parque nacional.
Se prevé que el costo total del proyecto supere los US$ 7.000 millones y será cubierto con los US$ 46.500 millones asignados a la construcción del muro fronterizo en la emblemática legislación de Trump, la “Gran y Hermosa Ley”.
Para acelerar el proceso, el Departamento de Seguridad Nacional eximió al proyecto del cumplimiento de numerosas leyes que protegen los recursos ambientales, históricos y culturales, entre ellas la Ley de Especies en Peligro de Extinción y la Ley de Agua Limpia. Este año se han presentado al menos cuatro demandas que buscan impugnar o frustrar el proyecto fronterizo del Gobierno en la región de Big Bend.
Los opositores a las obras dijeron a CNN que recibían con satisfacción la suspensión ordenada por Scott y su visita, pero se mostraron cautelosos sobre el resultado.
Jeff Leach, propietario de Basecamp Terlingua en Terlingua, cerca del parque nacional, dijo: “Esto demuestra que defender nuestras tierras públicas sí funciona”.
“Si él (Rodney Scott) no cambia el rumbo después de la visita, eso solo demostrará lo corrupto e inepto que ha sido todo el proceso. Si no hace nada, este lugar va a estallar y la presión nacional no hará más que aumentar”.
Billy Bartko, propietario de Far Flung Outdoor Center, que ofrece excursiones guiadas por el río y opera en el parque nacional desde hace 50 años, expresó opiniones similares.
“Es inquietante que esta sea la primera vez que viene a hablar con nosotros. Ya alteraron el parque y lo hicieron sin ninguna planificación. Apesta a irresponsabilidad”, agregó. “Esto debió hacerse antes de que soltaran las excavadoras en el Parque Nacional Big Bend”.
Bartko forma parte de una nueva demanda que busca una orden de restricción temporal contra el plan fronterizo de la administración de Trump para el parque nacional y otros tramos incluidos en el proyecto general. En una declaración presentada junto con la moción, Bartko argumentó que las obras en el parque podrían afectar su negocio al alterar el paisaje remoto y tranquilo que los clientes esperan disfrutar.
La demanda también incluye a People of La Junta for Preservation, un grupo que preserva lugares indígenas, y a Christina Hernandez, integrante de la Tribu Apache Lipán que considera que el plan fronterizo vulnera sus libertades religiosas. Hernandez afirma que practica una religión indígena vinculada a la geografía de la zona y que tiene previsto participar en un nuevo entierro religioso en un cementerio tradicional situado dentro del corredor propuesto para el muro fronterizo. Sostiene que el proyecto fronterizo del Gobierno impediría el acceso a lugares donde practica su religión.
